name: Backblaze B2 Cloud Storage
summary: Low-cost object storage on Backblaze’s own hardware, with its own API and an S3-compatible one.
intro: B2 keeps files on hardware Backblaze designs and runs itself. Storage Pods, servers packed with hard drives, are grouped into Vaults of 20, and each file is split into 17 data shards and 3 parity shards spread across the 20 pods, so a Vault can lose three whole pods without losing data. There are two ways in. The B2 Native API starts with `b2_authorize_account`, which returns a token; to upload, the client calls `b2_get_upload_url` and sends the bytes straight to the Vault that URL points at, so there is no central load balancer in the way. Since 2020 the same buckets also answer an S3-compatible API at `https://s3.<region>.backblazeb2.com`, which covers common tools but leaves out object ACLs, IAM roles, object tagging, website configuration and browser POST uploads. An account’s data lives in one of four regions (US West, US East, EU Central in Amsterdam, CA East in Toronto), picked at sign-up and fixed after that.

Pricing is storage-led. Since 1 May 2026 B2 costs $6.95 per TB-month (it was $6), the first 10 GB is free, and there are no minimum storage duration or minimum file size fees. Standard API calls are free for pay-as-you-go customers. Downloads are free up to three times your average stored data each month and $0.01 per GB beyond that, except through partner CDNs and clouds such as Cloudflare, Fastly, bunny.net and Vultr, where they stay free. B2 Overdrive, aimed at AI and high-performance computing, starts at $15 per TB-month with unlimited free egress. Backblaze, which also sells computer backup, is listed on NASDAQ as BLZE.
strengths: The lowest list price per TB in the comparison below, with no minimum duration or minimum object size, so short-lived data isn’t penalised
Downloads free up to three times your stored data, and unlimited through partners such as Cloudflare and Fastly
Standard API calls cost nothing, so millions of small requests don’t add up
A long public record: open Storage Pod designs since 2009 and drive failure statistics from its fleet since 2014
limits: The region is fixed per account at sign-up; moving means a new account and re-uploading, or paying for Cloud Replication while data sits in two places
The S3 API is partial: no object-level ACLs, IAM roles, object tagging, static website configuration or browser POST uploads
Egress beyond three times the stored data costs $0.01 per GB unless it goes through a partner, so a download-heavy public bucket can still pay for bandwidth
Only four regions, and prices have risen: $5 per TB at launch, $6 until April 2026, $6.95 since

sections.title: Getting data out without paying for it
sections.intro: B2’s egress rules reward steady storage and punish bursts of downloads. These are the ways the pricing page lists to stay at zero.

items.name: Stay under 3×
items.text: Each month you can download up to three times your average stored data free. A 10 TB bucket can serve 30 TB a month before the $0.01 per GB rate starts.

items.name: Serve through a partner CDN
items.text: Egress to these CDNs is free beyond the 3× allowance. With Cloudflare in front of a public bucket, Backblaze charges no download fees and Cloudflare caches the files.

items.name: Compute at a partner cloud
items.text: Reading data into machines at these providers is free too, so the bucket can sit at Backblaze while the compute runs elsewhere.

items.name: B2 Overdrive
items.text: A higher-priced tier for AI and high-performance computing that includes unlimited free egress.

story: Backblaze was founded in 2007 to sell unlimited computer backup for $5 a month. That only worked if raw storage was cheap, and off-the-shelf systems, from Amazon S3 to SAN arrays, cost “10 times as much (or more) than the raw hard drives”. So in September 2009 the company published the design of its own Storage Pod, a 4U server with 45 drives holding 67 TB for about $7,867 in parts, running Debian and the JFS file system, and invited others to copy and improve it. In January 2014 it began publishing failure rates for the tens of thousands of drives in its fleet, the start of its Drive Stats reports.

In 2015 Backblaze grouped pods into Vaults, 20 pods that each hold one shard of every file, and on 22 September Gleb Budman announced B2: the same storage, sold directly, at $0.005 per GB-month and $0.05 per GB downloaded, with uploads free. “Our storage systems were large enough, the tech advanced enough, and the team large enough to pull this off,” he wrote.

B2 launched with its own API. In May 2020 Backblaze added an S3-compatible one, Budman’s “most requested feature”, so S3 tools could switch by changing an endpoint. The company went public on NASDAQ in November 2021 with about 2 exabytes under management.

choices.why: Commercial storage cost ten times the drives inside it, which an unlimited $5 backup plan couldn’t carry. Years of publishing its designs and operational data also brought requests to use that storage directly, which became B2.
Splitting each file into 17 data and 3 parity shards on separate pods survives three pod failures at once with about 18% extra storage, where three full copies would need 200%.

choices.choice: Clients upload straight to a Vault
choices.why: The native API hands each client a URL for a specific Vault, so traffic doesn’t funnel through a central gateway and capacity grows by adding Vaults.

choices.choice: A native API first, S3 later
choices.why: B2 launched in 2015 with its own simpler API. Customers kept asking for S3 so their existing software would work, and it arrived in 2020.
